title: Toad in the Hole
subtitle: Pork sausages baked in a risen Yorkshire pudding batter
excerpt: Toad in the hole is pork sausages baked inside a Yorkshire pudding batter until the batter rises and puffs around the sausages in a hot, smoky tin. The result is a dramatic-looking dish with crisp, eggy batter at the edges and tender sausage in the centre. The batter must rest, the tin must be very hot, and the oven door must stay shut.
sourceNotes: Toad in the hole is first recorded in British cookbooks from the mid-eighteenth century, initially with cheaper cuts of meat baked in batter. The sausage version became the standard by the Victorian period and remains unchanged today.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make and rest the batter up to 24 hours ahead in the fridge. Bring to room temperature before using.

content.text: Toad in the hole rises or falls on the temperature of the tin when the batter goes in. The fat must be smoking; the batter must go in fast and the door must shut immediately. A cool tin gives you flat, oily batter. A properly hot tin gives you a puffed, golden Yorkshire pudding that engulfs the sausages. Rest the batter for at least an hour to let the flour hydrate fully.

Sift {{plain-flour}} of plain flour into a bowl with a pinch of salt. Make a well in the centre and add {{eggs}} eggs. Whisk together, then gradually whisk in {{whole-milk}} of milk until you have a smooth, thin batter with no lumps. Rest in the fridge for at least 1 hour.

Heat the oven to 220°C fan. Put the sunflower oil into a large roasting tin (about 30 x 20 cm) and heat in the oven for 10 minutes until smoking. Add the sausages directly to the hot fat and return to the oven for 10 minutes to brown.

Pull the tin out and, working very quickly, pour the rested batter evenly around the sausages. The fat should sizzle immediately. Slide back into the oven and bake for 25 to 28 minutes until the batter is puffed and deeply golden. Do not open the oven door in the first 20 minutes. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The batter has not risen and is flat
items.cause: The tin was not hot enough when the batter went in, or the oven door was opened too early.
items.fix: The fat must be smoking before the batter is added. Check that the oven has reached temperature and resist opening the door in the first 20 minutes.

items.symptom: The bottom of the batter is raw and pale
items.cause: The tin was too deep, or the batter was too thick.
items.fix: Use a wide, shallow tin so the batter spreads thin enough to cook through from below. A roasting tin, not a cake tin, is the right vessel.

items.symptom: The batter has collapsed after coming out of the oven
items.cause: The batter was not fully set when the oven was opened.
items.fix: Bake for the full 25 to 28 minutes. The batter will sink a little when served , this is normal and not a sign it failed.

items.symptom: The sausages are raw in the centre
items.cause: The sausages were not browned for long enough before the batter was added, and the batter-cooking time was insufficient.
items.fix: Brown the sausages for at least 10 minutes before adding the batter. The combined time of browning plus baking should cook any standard pork sausage through.

content.text: Toad in the hole is one of those British dishes with a name so odd that it has become a defining curiosity of the cuisine to anyone outside it. The name dates to the eighteenth century and has never been satisfactorily explained. The dish itself is a celebration of economy: cheap sausages and a batter of mostly flour, eggs, and milk that produces a result more generous-looking than its ingredients suggest. Serve with onion gravy and mashed potato.
